text.p: The following are the main stories from Thursday morning's Austrian newspapers:
- From January 1, 1998, women will be able to become soldiers in the Austrian army on a voluntary basis.

- Former Austrian chancellor Franz Vranitzky is prepared to take over the helm for the OSCE's operation in Albania. The 54-member states reached broad agreement on Wednesday to establish a humanitarian mission in Albania but failed to find common ground on a foreign protection force.

- Concerning Austria's joining NATO, Chancellor Viktor Klima said he not only wants a referendum to decide whether Austria should give up its neutrality, but also a referendum on any changes to the country's security policy.
- Austria will get new dialling codes from January 1, 1998 onwards when the postal system loses its telephone monopoly.
- Supermarket chains Julius Meinl and Billa have taken Toblerone chocolate bars off the shelves after it became known that they contain genetically-modified lecithin.
- Economos sells its Hamburg-based Merkel to Germany's Freudenberg group.
- Mayr-Melnhof buys Reynolds' German cigarette packaging plant and sees extra sales of 1.5 billion schillings from the purchase.
- Radex-Heraklith manages to turn in substantial improvement in 1996 earnings and expects the current year to be even better.
- All genetically-modified products will have to be labelled as such from April 2 in Austria.
- Sending a force to Albania could cost the Austrian army 100 million schillings, which it does not have, said Austria's highest ranking officer.
- GiroCredit supervisory board chief Rene Alfons Haiden says postal savings bank PSK would be an ideal completion of Die Erste and GiroCredit.
- Austria's ailing tourism industry suffers bad February, when overnight stays slumped dramatically.
- Radex-Heraklith raises its dividend by one schilling to 15 schillings after announcing a strong set of 1996 earnings.
